title: {{NAME}} and the Final Whistle at the Edge of the Sky
moral: True strength is not about winning alone, but about lifting others so the whole team can fly.

pages.content:
The stadium appeared without warning on the morning of {{NAME}}'s birthday, rising from the empty lot at the end of Ferndale Road like a dream somebody had forgotten to put away. Its walls were woven from clouds, its floodlights were captured lightning bolts humming softly in their casings, and the grass on the pitch shimmered with the same faint iridescence you see in a puddle after rain.

A banner the size of a small country stretched above the entrance arch. It read, in letters that rearranged themselves whenever {{NAME}} looked away, THE SKYWARD CUP, and below that, smaller, INVITED PLAYERS ONLY. A fairy no bigger than a thumbprint sat perched on the final P, polishing her wings with a corner of the banner.

Her name was Zorra. She wore a referee's outfit scaled precisely to her tiny frame, complete with a whistle so small it looked like a grain of rice on a chain, and she carried a clipboard that somehow held the names of every player who had ever dreamed hard enough about football to deserve a place here.

{{NAME}}'s name was at the very top.

'Took you long enough,' Zorra said, tucking her pen behind a pointed ear. 'The others are already warming up.'

pages.content:
The warm-up pitch was absolute chaos, in the best possible way.

Two superheroes were practicing headers. One, a stocky girl named Vela, wore a cape the colour of thunderstorms and could, apparently, redirect the ball mid-air with a single concentrated look. The other, a tall boy with silver gauntlets named Cassian, kept accidentally kicking the ball into orbit and then catching it again before it could leave the atmosphere.

'He's still working on the calibration,' Vela said, shaking her head with the weary affection of someone who has explained this many times.

Zorra zoomed between them like a furious little meteor, blowing her grain-of-rice whistle. More fairies emerged from the grass itself, springing up wherever a cleat touched the ground, each one trailing a different colour of light. They fixed divots, re-chalked the lines, and argued loudly in voices that sounded like champagne glasses clinking.

{{NAME}} stood at the edge of it all, taking it in, his heart hammering in his chest like a very enthusiastic drum. He had played football in muddy parks and drizzly school yards. He had never once played under lightning-bolt floodlights on a cloud-woven pitch while a thunderstorm-caped superhero gave him a measuring look.

'You're the one Zorra picked specially,' Vela said. Not a question. 'Can you actually play?'

{{NAME}} took a slow breath. 'Yes,' he said simply.

pages.content:
The match was unlike anything gravity usually permitted.

Vela used her powers precisely once, in the thirty-second minute, redirecting a shot that was heading straight for their own goal, and then refused to do it again. 'That would be cheating,' she said, almost annoyed that anyone had suggested otherwise.

Cassian, for his part, was a revelation without his gauntlets, which Zorra had confiscated before kickoff. He was fast and clever and laughed too loudly every time he lost the ball, which somehow made him better rather than worse.

{{NAME}} played the way he always played, which was with every part of himself at once. He tracked runs, held the line, slipped passes through gaps that shouldn't have been there. The fairies cheered from the touchline with the ferocity of a thousand tiny opera audiences, and Zorra blew her whistle so often that it started to sound like birdsong.

With three minutes left and the score level, {{NAME}} found himself alone, one-on-one with the keeper. The cloudstuff pitch swirled around his boots. The lightning-bolt floodlights blazed. He had the shot.

But Cassian was in a better position, unmarked, screaming for the ball.

{{NAME}} passed.

Cassian scored. The fairies erupted from the grass in a fountain of coloured light.

pages.content:
They won. Obviously they won. But that was not the hard part.

The hard part came right after, in the hushed tunnel beneath the stands, where Zorra pulled {{NAME}} aside with surprising force for someone the size of a thumb.

'You had that goal,' she said. Her tiny face was very serious. 'Everyone saw it. Why?'

{{NAME}} thought about the look on Cassian's face when he'd scored. Not triumph, exactly. Something bigger and messier. Like joy and surprise and belonging, all at once.

'Cassian's been trying to play without using his powers,' {{NAME}} said slowly. 'All game. If he'd scored because I did something brilliant, that would be about me. If he scored because he was brilliant, that's about him.' He paused. 'That seemed more important.'

Zorra stared at him for a very long moment. Then she put two fingers in her mouth and produced a whistle-blast that, from someone her size, was frankly unreasonable.

Vela appeared instantly. Then Cassian. Then approximately forty fairies, descending from the rafters like a very festive ceiling.

Cassian grabbed {{NAME}} by the shoulders. His silver gauntlets were back on, Zorra having returned them, and his grip was accidentally much stronger than intended. 'I've been trying to score without my powers for six games,' he said. 'Six games.'

'I know,' {{NAME}} said. 'I watched you figure it out.'

pages.content:
The Skyward Cup trophy was made of solid cloudstone, cool and faintly luminous, and it was passed from hand to hand until everyone had held it, including all forty fairies, which took considerably longer than expected.

Zorra delivered a speech from atop the trophy itself. It lasted four minutes and contained, by {{NAME}}'s count, eleven different dramatic pauses.

By the time the stadium began to thin and the cloud walls dissolved softly back into the morning sky, {{NAME}} was comfortably exhausted in a way that lives in your legs and your chest and somewhere behind your eyes. He walked home with grass stains on his royal blue shorts and a fairy-light smudge on one emerald cleat that refused to come off no matter how he rubbed it.

His mum said nothing about the grass stains, which meant she had noticed something about his face that was more interesting.

He fell asleep quickly and warmly, the cloudstone-cool memory of the trophy still in his palms.

And just before sleep arrived completely, he heard, from somewhere tiny and outside his window, the unmistakable silver-bell sound of Zorra's whistle.

One short sharp blast.

The kind that means: get some rest. The next match starts at dawn.
